notes.h: Key terms: planning, renewal and redevelopment
points: Urban planning: controlling the use and development of land through development plans, zoning, planning permission and public investment.
Urban renewal: improving and rehabilitating existing run-down areas, keeping the community in place.
Urban redevelopment: clearing an area completely and rebuilding it, often with new uses and new people.
Renewal improves what is already there, while redevelopment clears and rebuilds. Ballymun and Limerick combined both, while the Docklands was mainly redevelopment.
Gentrification can be a side-effect of renewal or redevelopment: better-off people move in, prices rise and original residents are displaced.
Development plans and zoning, which decide the uses permitted in each area.
Tax incentives in designated areas, which reduce the cost of restoring or building in the area.
Special development agencies with planning powers: the Dublin Docklands Development Authority (DDDA) and the London Docklands Development Corporation (LDDC).
Strategic Development Zones: fast-track planning for areas of national importance.

Part V of the Planning and Development Act 2000: a requirement that part of new housing development be social and affordable housing. Up to 20% of land zoned for housing could be required for this purpose. The share was reduced to 10% in 2015 and restored to 20% by the Affordable Housing Act 2021. Strategic Development Zones are created under the same Act.
Derelict and vacant sites levies, which charge owners of unused property to encourage its reuse.
Public transport investment, to link new and renewed areas to the rest of the city.
New towns, planned as new settlements away from the existing city.
Regeneration companies with community participation, which bring residents into decisions about their area.

notes.b: The Advisory Regional Plan for Dublin, by Myles Wright in 1967, proposed the western new towns of Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown.
points: What it did: it housed rapid growth in new towns on the western edge of Dublin.
Effectiveness: the towns were built before services, jobs and transport, so their residents depended on distant jobs and facilities.
Tallaght's shopping centre, The Square, opened only in 1990, and the Luas Red Line to Tallaght opened in 2004, decades after the first homes.
Criticism: the plan produced sprawl and the absence of community, because the towns lacked the facilities that would have made them places in their own right.

notes.h: National strategic plans: National Spatial Strategy (2002)
points: What it did: named nine gateways (Dublin, Cork, Limerick/Shannon, Galway, Waterford, Dundalk, Sligo, Letterkenny with Derry, and Athlone–Tullamore–Mullingar) and nine hubs, to balance growth away from Dublin.
The 2003 Budget announced a decentralisation programme that moved civil servants to dozens of towns.
Effectiveness: weakened by too many designated centres, by decentralisation to towns not named in the plan, and by the property boom.
Dublin continued to sprawl, so the plan did not achieve its aim of balancing growth.
The strategy was replaced in 2018 by the National Planning Framework.

notes.h: National strategic plans: National Planning Framework (2018)
notes.b: The National Planning Framework, known as Project Ireland 2040, was published in 2018.
points: Plans for about 1 million more people in Ireland by 2040.
Half of future population growth to be in Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford, the five cities.
Galway, Cork, Limerick and Waterford are each to grow by at least 50%.
Compact growth: 40% of new homes nationally to be within the built-up footprint of existing settlements, on brownfield and infill land.
Regional Spatial and Economic Strategies, prepared by the three regional assemblies.
The Urban Regeneration and Development Fund was set up in 2018.
Effectiveness: too early to judge fully, but housing supply has lagged behind the targets.

notes.b: Housing is one of three urban problems (with transport and pollution) on which planning effectiveness is judged. The strategies are the Part V requirement, Rent Pressure Zones and national housing targets.
points: Housing for All (2021) set a target of an average of about 33,000 new homes a year to 2030.
Rent Pressure Zones were introduced in December 2016, first in Dublin and Cork, to limit rent increases.
Part V social and affordable housing, described under Tools available to planners, adds homes within private developments.
Effectiveness: completions have risen, but they have stayed below the level of need.
Over 15,000 people were in State-funded emergency accommodation in 2025, a record level of homelessness.
High rents remain a problem, showing that the strategies have not yet matched demand.

notes.b: The transport strategy covers public transport investment and cycling, with the aim of reducing congestion.
points: DART opened in 1984, and the Luas Cross City linked the Red and Green lines through the city centre in December 2017.
The Port Tunnel opened in 2006, and the 2007 restriction on heavy goods vehicles kept most five-axle lorries out of the city centre.
Dublin Bikes was launched in 2009, and BusConnects is the bus network redesign.
The NTA Greater Dublin Area Transport Strategy 2022 to 2042 sets out the long-term plan.
Effectiveness: the Luas and the Port Tunnel succeeded in their aims.

Metro North, a planned rail line to Dublin Airport and Swords, was shelved by the Government in 2011. Its successor, MetroLink, is planned but has been repeatedly delayed, and no date or cost is yet set.
Congestion persists because land use remains dispersed, so people still need cars to reach jobs and shops.
Smoky coal ban: introduced in Dublin on 1 September 1990 and extended nationwide in October 2022.
Plastic bag levy, introduced in 2002, which cut plastic bag use sharply.
Ringsend wastewater treatment plant upgrade, to reduce discharges into Dublin Bay.
Clean Air Strategy, published in 2023.
Effectiveness: smoke and smog were largely removed after the coal ban.
Limits: traffic nitrogen dioxide and particulates from solid fuel remain problems.

notes.b: The Docklands were derelict after the docks lost their trade to containerisation. Renewal there was mainly redevelopment, clearing and rebuilding the area.
points: Actions: the Urban Renewal Act 1986 gave tax incentives in the designated area.
The Custom House Docks Development Authority was set up in 1986, and the International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) was set up in 1987.
The Dublin Docklands Development Authority was set up in 1997, and was wound up in 2016 with its functions passing to Dublin City Council.
Flagship projects: the Samuel Beckett Bridge (2009), the Convention Centre Dublin (2010), the Bord Gáis Energy Theatre (2010) and the Luas Red Line extension to The Point (2009).
A Strategic Development Zone covering North Lotts and Grand Canal Dock was designated in 2014.
Results: new offices, homes and culture venues, and the Docklands became a centre for tech firms, including Google's European headquarters at Grand Canal Dock, known as 'Silicon Docks'.
Criticism: early schemes favoured offices and expensive apartments, while local residents got few of the jobs created.
Criticism: social housing was slow to be built, and gentrification pushed up prices.
The DDDA was damaged by its role in the purchase of the Irish Glass Bottle site, Ringsend, in 2006 for about €412 million, at the peak of the property bubble. The land value collapsed after 2008.

notes.b: Temple Bar is a renewal case: an existing run-down area was improved and turned into a cultural quarter rather than cleared.
points: Problem: the CIÉ (the State transport company) planned a central bus station in Temple Bar in the 1980s, and bought up property in the area.
Artists and small businesses moved in on short leases, bringing new life to the area.
The bus station plan was dropped, and Temple Bar Properties was set up in 1991 under the Temple Bar Area Renewal and Development Act 1991.
Dublin was European City of Culture in 1991, which gave the area national attention.
Results: cultural venues, including the Irish Film Institute and the Project Arts Centre; restored buildings; and tourism.
Criticism: the area became dominated by pubs and night-time tourism, and few people live there permanently.

notes.b: Ballymun combined renewal and redevelopment. Its 1960s high-rise flats were replaced by new low-rise housing and a new town centre.
points: Problems: seven 15-storey towers built in 1966 to 1969 suffered isolation, poor maintenance, unemployment and drugs.
Ballymun Regeneration Ltd was set up by Dublin Corporation in 1997.
The towers were demolished between 2004 and 2015, and new low-rise homes were built.
New facilities included Main Street, the Axis arts and community centre, and an IKEA store, which opened in 2009 as IKEA's first store in the Republic of Ireland.
Effectiveness: housing quality improved, and residents were involved in the regeneration.
Limits: the recession stalled the town centre, the promised Metro North rail link was never built, and unemployment stayed high.

notes.b: Limerick Regeneration addresses estates of concentrated disadvantage, after the 2006 arson attack in Moyross and the 2007 report by John Fitzgerald.
points: Limerick Regeneration agencies were set up in 2007, and were later integrated into Limerick City and County Council, formed in 2014.
The programme covered Moyross, Southill, St Mary's Park and Ballinacurra Weston.
Actions: demolition of the worst estates, building of new homes, and social and economic programmes.
Criticism: the regeneration was slow, and demolition outpaced rebuilding.
Criticism: the populations of the estates fell during the process, as residents moved away.

notes.b: Adamstown, near Lucan in South Dublin, is a planned new suburb built as a Strategic Development Zone.
points: Designated a Strategic Development Zone in 2001, with fast-track planning.
Planned as a new suburb with its own railway station on the Kildare line, and with schools and services built in phases alongside the housing.
Effectiveness: a model of planned phasing, in which services arrive with the homes.
Development stalled after the 2008 property crash and resumed in the late 2010s, showing how much the scheme depended on the market.
Living City Initiative, introduced in 2015: tax relief for refurbishing older buildings in special regeneration areas of Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway, Waterford and Kilkenny, later extended.
Cork Area Strategic Plan, 2001, guided planning in the city.
The Cork city boundary was extended in 2019.
Luas Cork: a light rail line proposed in the Cork Metropolitan Area Transport Strategy of 2020. It is proposed only, and no cost, route length or opening date has been set.
Cork Docklands is the next large regeneration project in the city.

notes.b: The London Docklands were redeveloped after the docks closed in the 1960s to 1980s. The scheme was top-down, led by an agency with its own planning powers.
points: London Docklands Development Corporation, 1981 to 1998, was an unelected body with planning powers.
An Enterprise Zone on the Isle of Dogs gave tax breaks and simplified planning.
Canary Wharf was developed, with One Canada Square completed in 1991.
The Docklands Light Railway opened in 1987, and London City Airport opened in 1987.
The Jubilee Line extension opened in 1999.
Results: a second financial centre, jobs and housing.
Criticism: the corporation was top-down and bypassed local councils.
Criticism: jobs went to commuters from outside the area, while local residents were priced out, and transport came late.
The five new towns from the 1965 regional plan took growth away from the city of Paris.
The grands ensembles, large housing estates in the banlieues, became problem estates.
The Grand Paris Express, about 200 km of new automatic metro lines with 68 stations, aims to link the banlieues to the rest of the region.

notes.h: Overall evaluation of planning and renewal
points: Planning works best when housing, jobs, services and transport are delivered together, and when residents are involved in decisions.
Flagship property-led schemes create jobs and buildings, but do not always bring benefits to local people.
National plans are undermined when other policies pull in the opposite direction, such as tax incentives for development and decentralisation to towns outside the plan.

keyTerms.definition: The control of land use and development through development plans, zoning, planning permission and public investment.
The improvement and rehabilitation of existing run-down areas, keeping the community in place.
The complete clearance of an area and its rebuilding, often with new uses and new residents.
The movement of better-off people into an area, raising prices and displacing original residents.
An area of national importance designated for fast-track planning.
The provision of the Planning and Development Act 2000 requiring part of new housing development to be social and affordable housing.
An area, first introduced in 2016, where rent increases are limited.
The 2002 plan that named gateways and hubs to balance growth away from Dublin.
The 2018 national plan, known as Project Ireland 2040, which sets out population growth and compact growth targets.
An area with tax breaks and simplified planning, used to attract development, such as the Isle of Dogs in London.
The moving of government jobs out of the capital to towns and cities elsewhere.
A rail line planned to Dublin Airport and Swords, shelved in 2011.

factCards.term: Wright Report 1967: what it did and how effective it was
factCards.definition: Planned the western new towns of Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown, housing rapid growth. But homes came before services, jobs and transport (The Square, Tallaght, opened in 1990; the Luas in 2004), causing sprawl and absence of community.

factCards.term: National Spatial Strategy 2002: aims and why it fell short
factCards.definition: It named gateways, including Dublin, Cork, Limerick/Shannon, Galway, Waterford, Dundalk and Sligo, and hubs to balance growth. Weakened by too many centres, the 2003 decentralisation to towns not in the plan and the property boom; Dublin kept sprawling; replaced in 2018.

factCards.term: National Planning Framework 2018: four key targets
factCards.definition: About 1 million more people by 2040; half of growth in Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford; Galway, Cork, Limerick and Waterford each to grow by at least 50%; 40% of new homes within the built-up footprint of existing settlements.

factCards.term: National Planning Framework: delivery tools and effectiveness so far
factCards.definition: Regional Spatial and Economic Strategies prepared by the three regional assemblies; the Urban Regeneration and Development Fund, set up in 2018. It is too early to judge fully, but housing supply has lagged behind the targets.

factCards.term: Housing strategies: what they are and how effective they have been
factCards.definition: Housing for All (2021): about 33,000 new homes a year to 2030; Rent Pressure Zones from December 2016, first in Dublin and Cork; Part V. Completions rose but stayed below need; over 15,000 people in emergency accommodation in 2025; high rents.

factCards.term: Transport strategies in Dublin: successes and failures
factCards.definition: Success: the Luas (2004) and Luas Cross City (2017); the Port Tunnel (2006) and 2007 lorry restriction; Dublin Bikes (2009). Limits: Metro North shelved in 2011 and MetroLink repeatedly delayed; congestion persists as land use is still dispersed.

factCards.term: Pollution strategies: what worked and what problems remain
factCards.definition: The smoky coal ban (Dublin 1990, nationwide 2022) largely removed smoke and smog; plastic bag levy (2002); Ringsend upgrade for Dublin Bay; Clean Air Strategy (2023). Still problems: traffic nitrogen dioxide and particulates from solid fuel.

factCards.term: Dublin Docklands: redevelopment actions with dates
factCards.definition: Urban Renewal Act 1986 tax incentives; Custom House Docks Development Authority, 1986; IFSC set up 1987; Dublin Docklands Development Authority, 1997–2016; North Lotts and Grand Canal Dock Strategic Development Zone, 2014.

factCards.term: Dublin Docklands: flagship projects and results
factCards.definition: Samuel Beckett Bridge and the Luas extension to The Point (2009); Convention Centre Dublin and Bord Gáis Energy Theatre (2010); new offices, homes and culture venues; tech firms in Silicon Docks, including Google's European headquarters at Grand Canal Dock.

factCards.term: Dublin Docklands: criticisms
factCards.definition: Offices and costly apartments came first; locals got few jobs; social housing was slow; gentrification raised prices; the DDDA was damaged by its role in buying the Irish Glass Bottle site, Ringsend, in 2006 for about €412 million, at the peak of the bubble.

factCards.term: Temple Bar: how it was renewed, and criticisms
factCards.definition: CIÉ bought property in the 1980s for a bus station; artists moved in on short leases; the plan was dropped and Temple Bar Properties (1991) made a cultural quarter (Irish Film Institute, Project Arts Centre). Criticism: pubs, night-time tourism, few residents.

factCards.term: Ballymun regeneration: actions with dates
factCards.definition: Ballymun Regeneration Ltd was set up by Dublin Corporation in 1997; the seven 15-storey towers (1966–69) were demolished 2004–2015; new low-rise homes, Main Street, the Axis arts and community centre, and IKEA's first Republic of Ireland store (2009).

factCards.term: Ballymun regeneration: how effective was it?
factCards.definition: Success: housing quality improved and residents were involved in the regeneration. Limits: the recession stalled the town centre; the promised Metro North rail link was shelved in 2011 and never built; unemployment stayed high.

factCards.term: Limerick Regeneration: actions and criticisms
factCards.definition: Agencies set up in 2007 after the Fitzgerald report demolished and rebuilt housing in Moyross, Southill, St Mary's Park and Ballinacurra Weston, with social and economic programmes. Criticism: slow; demolition outpaced rebuilding; estate populations fell.

factCards.term: Adamstown: why it is a model and what went wrong
factCards.definition: Near Lucan, South Dublin: a Strategic Development Zone from 2001 with its own station on the Kildare line, and schools and services phased in alongside housing. Building stalled after the 2008 crash and resumed in the late 2010s.

factCards.term: Smaller-city renewal: the Living City Initiative and Cork
factCards.definition: Living City Initiative, 2015: tax relief to refurbish older buildings in Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway, Waterford and Kilkenny. Cork: Area Strategic Plan 2001; boundary extended 2019; Luas Cork proposed (2020 strategy); Cork Docklands the next big scheme.

factCards.term: London Docklands: redevelopment actions with dates
factCards.definition: London Docklands Development Corporation, 1981–1998, an unelected body with planning powers; Enterprise Zone on the Isle of Dogs; Docklands Light Railway and London City Airport, 1987; One Canada Square, Canary Wharf, 1991; Jubilee Line extension, 1999.

factCards.term: London Docklands: results and criticisms
factCards.definition: Results: a second financial centre, jobs and housing. Criticisms: the corporation was top-down and bypassed local councils; jobs went to commuters from outside the area; local residents were priced out; transport came late.

factCards.term: Paris planning: three responses and their outcomes
factCards.definition: Five new towns from the 1965 plan took growth from the city; the grands ensembles in the banlieues became problem estates; the Grand Paris Express, about 200 km of new automatic metro lines with 68 stations, aims to link the banlieues.

factCards.term: Urban planning and renewal: three conclusions on effectiveness
factCards.definition: Planning works best when housing, jobs, services and transport arrive together and residents are involved; flagship property-led schemes bring jobs and buildings but not always local benefits; national plans fail when other policies pull against them.

questions.prompt: Examine the effectiveness of urban planning strategies in solving two of the following urban problems: housing; transport; pollution.
questions.model: Housing: 1. Housing for All (2021) set a target of about 33,000 new homes a year to 2030; its success is limited because completions have risen but stayed below need. 2. Rent Pressure Zones, introduced in December 2016 first in Dublin and Cork, limit rent increases, but high rents remain. 3. Part V requires a share of new private housing development to be social and affordable housing; the share was cut to 10% in 2015 and restored to 20% by the Affordable Housing Act 2021, so its effect has depended on policy changes. 4. The National Planning Framework (2018) aims for 40% of new homes within existing built-up areas, but it is too early to judge and housing supply has lagged. 5. Over 15,000 people were in State-funded emergency accommodation in 2025, showing the strategies have not solved homelessness. 6. Limit: the Wright Report (1967) western new towns housed growth but were built before services and transport, creating sprawl and absence of community. Transport: 7. The Luas (2004) and the Luas Cross City (December 2017) improved public transport across the city. 8. The Port Tunnel (2006) and the 2007 restriction on heavy goods vehicles removed port traffic from the centre. 9. Dublin Bikes (2009) and BusConnects give alternatives to the car. 10. The NTA Greater Dublin Area Transport Strategy 2022 to 2042 sets a long-term plan. 11. Limit: Metro North was shelved in 2011, and MetroLink is planned but has been repeatedly delayed. 12. Limit: congestion persists because land use is still dispersed, so many journeys still need cars. Conclusion: strategies have succeeded where they delivered a specific project, such as the Luas and the Port Tunnel, but have been weakest where housing and transport were not planned together with jobs and services.

questions.prompt: Assess the effectiveness of urban renewal in solving urban problems, with reference to examples you have studied.
questions.model: Dublin Docklands: 1. Problem: derelict docks after containerisation. 2. Action: the Urban Renewal Act 1986 gave tax incentives, the IFSC was set up in 1987, and the DDDA was set up in 1997. 3. Flagship projects: the Samuel Beckett Bridge (2009), the Convention Centre Dublin (2010) and the Luas Red Line extension to The Point (2009). 4. Results: new offices, homes, culture venues and tech firms, including Google's European headquarters at Grand Canal Dock. 5. Criticism: early schemes favoured offices and expensive apartments, local residents got few jobs, social housing was slow, and gentrification pushed up prices. 6. The DDDA's role in the purchase of the Irish Glass Bottle site in 2006, for about 412 million euro at the peak of the bubble, damaged its reputation after the land value collapsed. Ballymun: 7. Problems in the 1960s towers were isolation, poor maintenance, unemployment and drugs. 8. Action: the towers, built 1966 to 1969, were demolished 2004 to 2015 and replaced with low-rise homes, Main Street and the Axis centre. 9. Results: housing quality improved and residents were involved. 10. Criticism: the recession stalled the town centre, Metro North was shelved in 2011, and unemployment stayed high. Evaluation: renewal has been effective in physical improvement and the creation of jobs, but less effective in helping existing residents, because property-led schemes bring benefits unevenly and leave some problems unsolved.

questions.prompt: Explain briefly what is meant by urban renewal and urban redevelopment.
questions.model: Urban renewal is the improvement and rehabilitation of existing run-down areas, keeping the community in place. Example: Temple Bar in Dublin, where old buildings were restored and cultural venues created in the 1990s, with the artists and small businesses that moved in kept in the area. Urban redevelopment is the complete clearance of an area and its rebuilding, often with new uses and new people. Example: the Dublin Docklands, where derelict docks were cleared and replaced with offices, homes and cultural venues after containerisation.
